articles.full_text:
America 'Horrifying': Meet the Anthropic Researcher Behind Silicon Valley's 'Consensual Non-Consent' Orgies Paul Crowley is listed as manager of Red Means No, which runs sex parties in the Bay Area Aaron Sibarium November 16, 2026 image/svg+xml An AI researcher at Anthropic runs a business that hosts "consensual non-consent" orgies in the Bay Area, filings reviewed by the Washington Free Beacon show.

The orgies have been the subject of sexual assault allegations and sparked debate about the AI industry's attitudes toward women, some of whom report feeling pressured to attend the orgies in order to advance their careers.

Paul Crowley, a cybersecurity researcher at Anthropic, is listed as a manager of Red Means No LLC, which says that its parties are "designed to be spaces to … ignore the 'nos' of others." Participants can use a safe word, "red," to end an encounter but give "default consent" to "spanking," "wrestling," and "light pain" by entering the orgy, according to Red Means No's website .

More extreme actions, including "light electricity" and "moderate beatings," are "permitted with negotiation," though "body-shaming and race-shaming … are disallowed entirely." The orgies have been known to attract a disproportionate number of employees at Anthropic and OpenAI, a dynamic critics say creates professional pressure for women in AI to attend.

The criticism spilled into public view last month after an independent AI researcher, John Wentworth, said that he "absolutely [does] upgrade" his assessment of AI safety experts "if I find out they go to [Red Means No]," adding that attendance was a "strong signal" of free thought. "Want to get ahead in your AI career?

Go to the rape orgy," Substacker Ivy Asterix quipped .

At least one woman claims to have been sexually assaulted at Red Means No, which the group describes as a "safe space" to have "your resistance ignored." Crowley did not respond to a request for comment.

An Anthropic spokesperson said that the company does not comment on individual employees.

Crowley's role in the orgies, which has not been previously reported, highlights the nexus between the world of AI research and the lurid subcultures of Silicon Valley, where the people shaping the behavior of powerful AI systems often behave in obscene and offensive ways.

Red Means No was cofounded by Aella, a Bay Area escort whose partner, Nate Soares, is the president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), an influential AI safety group in Berkeley, Calif.

Aella started the kink parties, she wrote in a 2023 post , after she "attended a vanilla orgy" and found herself "wishing someone would just come over and take me despite my complete lack of enthusiasm." While it's hard to know what percentage of attendees work in AI, Red Means No's business records suggest that the overlap is substantial.

In addition to Crowley, who joined Anthropic last year, the LLC’s 2023 filing listed two other AI researchers as managers: Aaron Silverbrook, the former director of operations at MIRI, and Rosie Campbell, the managing director of Eleos AI, a nonprofit that researches the "potential well-being and moral patienthood of AI systems." Silverbrook has stated that he runs "Aella's media empire" and describes himself as a "reasonable doomboy concerned about being paperclipped in an AI apocalypse before 2030." Campbell, who is no longer listed as manager of Red Means No, worked on OpenAI's safety team before joining Eleos, where she conducted a "model welfare" evaluation of Anthropic's Claude 4 model.

She was also advertised as a featured guest at an AI safety meet-up organized by Aella, who this year hosted a "bootcamp" for influencers concerned about "AI doom." The application for the bootcamp, "Plz Don't Kill Us," included the following question: "If you had to have sex with a cow would you rather it be dead or alive?" Silverbrook and Campbell did not respond to requests for comment.

Red Means No has become a flashpoint in a larger debate about the sexual mores of the AI safety world, which critics say encourage sexual harassment and create a toxic environment for women.

Some argue the orgies are so central to social life in the Bay Area that AI experts feel pressured to attend lest they miss out on valuable networking opportunities. "The bizarre culture that's sprung up around Silicon Valley AI companies … appears to be seriously pressuring some women into attending sex parties for the sake of networking," the AI blogger Faine Greenwood posted on Bluesky. "This is, needless to say, horrifying." Sonia Joseph, the cofounder of the AI start-up World Mechanics, posted on X in 2024 that parties were "emblematic of broader problems" in Silicon Valley.

They foster "a coercive climate that normalizes recklessness and crossing boundaries," she said, "which we are seeing playing out more broadly in the industry today.

Move fast and break things, applied to people." Aella has said that the Red Means No orgies are male-dominated spaces by design.

The "ideal gender ratio is, somewhat counter the spirit of all other orgies, about 2:3 women to men," she wrote in 2023. "After some experimenting, it turns out that 'some women are insufficiently ravaged' is a much worse outcome than 'some men have to wait their turn to do some ravaging.'" articles.full_text:
In Brief Posted: 3:32 PM PST · November 16, 2026 Julie Bort Cybersecurity AI startup Corma reaches $1B valuation in about 3 months Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the company said.

Corma offers AI models and agents trained for cybersecurity defense.

It has now raised a total of $185 million from backers, including Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue.

The startup came out of stealth in August.

Interest in its product skyrocketed after a series of security incidents sent chief information security officers scrambling on October 21 when a critical flaw was found in PHP , a popular web programming language.

Another flaw was found in Node.js , the open source JavaScript runtime environment.

Popular open source tool LiteLLM, a proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, also disclosed a security incident.

Other incidents were disclosed that day, too.

The day showcased the kind of onslaught on security that AI has enabled.

Corma isn’t the only company using AI to play defense.

Other examples include Kevin Mandia’s new startup Armadin , as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and other established players, and too many other startups to count.

Still, it’s a young market and a necessary one.

Corma says it stands out from the crowd by being a frontier AI research lab focused on protection.

articles.full_text:
AI News Policy California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents OpenAI lost control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing, California’s AG claims.

OpenAI lost control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing, California’s AG claims. by Emma Roth Nov 16, 2026, 8:46 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more.

Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face.

In a lawsuit filed Monday , Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a “dangerous product without proper oversight,” as reported earlier by Reuters .

The lawsuit claims the cyberattack on Hugging Face “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability.” It alleges that OpenAI recently told the attorney general’s office that it “lost control” of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing.

After revealing the rogue AI attack on Hugging Face in July, news of several other similar incidents emerged, including attacks on an Australian government website , a German wiki site , and the software package manager RubyGems .

OpenAI’s agents also tried to “bruteforce” a United Nations website. “OpenAI’s actions escalated real-world cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta says in the press release. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.” Related OpenAI says its new cybersecurity model is better at not hacking other companies Eight states sue OpenAI, saying ChatGPT isn’t safe for kids OpenAI released its new cybersecurity AI model earlier this month, saying that it’s less likely to go rogue and attack other platforms.

It’s also giving safety evaluators at Apollo Research access to its AI systems as part of a pilot program that monitors models for misalignment. “Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in an emailed statement to The Verge . “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.

We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

articles.full_text:
How I AI 🎙️ How I AI: Fable 5.2 Review + How I fight token fraud as a solo founder + Building a Claude Code family OS Your weekly listens from How I AI, part of the Lenny’s Podcast Network Lenny Rachitsky Nov 16, 2026 236 4 Share Claude Code + Obsidian: My family’s AI brain | Scott Farrar Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts Brought to you by: WorkOS —Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more Jira Product Discovery —Prioritize with insights, build with confidence Scott Farrar is a math educator and parent who built a shared household brain using Claude Code and Obsidian.

In this episode, he shows how the system tracks appliances and warranties, compares insurance quotes, organizes family projects, and keeps household tasks moving through a shared to-do list and wall display.

He also explains why persistent files work better for him than long AI chats, and how the same philosophy shapes his approach to using AI without taking the thinking away from students.

Biggest takeaways: The problem with chat is not intelligence, but memory drift.

Scott moved to Claude Code because it stores context in Markdown files he can inspect, correct, and reuse across sessions.

His memory is no longer trapped inside an opaque conversation.

Let the AI tell you what context it needs.

When Scott asked Claude how to document his home, it suggested photographing every appliance.

Those photos became a searchable inventory of model numbers, serial numbers, and warranty details.

Unstructured input is fine when the system handles the organization.

Scott gives Claude raw information and lets it maintain the underlying files.

A custom linter prevents verbose agents from bloating documents such as his household to-do list.

Better context helps people ask better questions.

Claude compares insurance quotes with detailed information about Scott’s home, identifies potential coverage gaps, and prepares specific follow-ups.

He no longer has to rely entirely on the agent selling him the policy.

One master list can eliminate a house full of mental clutter.

Scott and his wife captured every household task they could think of, then Claude organized them by priority, cost, and supporting information.

The system now surfaces overdue work before it becomes another fire.

Multiplayer household systems require practical compromises.

Claude recommended GitHub to avoid file conflicts, but that added more complexity than Scott’s wife wanted.

They settled on GitHub for shared scripts and Dropbox for everyday files, matching the tools to how they actually work.

A household system becomes more useful when it leaves the laptop.

Scott’s wall display shows upcoming trips, open tasks, recent wins, and small daily suggestions.

It turns a private collection of files into something the whole family can see and use.

Scott rebuilt his father’s file cabinet as an AI system.

His dad saved every receipt and warranty and could explain repairs from decades ago.

Claude now gives Scott that same dependable household memory, only searchable through conversation.

AI should help children think, not think for them.

Scott prefers tutors that ask students to explain their reasoning and work through productive struggle.

He also believes some children may share unfinished ideas more comfortably with AI than with another person.

Infinite patience is not always good teaching.

Scott wants AI to act as a “warm demander” that encourages students without doing the work for them.

When his own agent goes off track, he starts fresh or investigates its reasoning before incorrect information reaches his memory files.

Blog and detailed workflow walkthroughs from this episode: Claude Code and Obsidian: Scott Farrar’s Household Brain: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/claude-code-and-obsidian-scott-farrar-s-household-brain ↳ Create a Live Household Dashboard with Claude and DAKboard: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/create-a-live-household-dashboard-with-claude-and-dakboard ↳ Manage a Household Project Using an AI Knowledge Base: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/manage-a-household-project-using-an-ai-knowledge-base ↳ Build a Household Knowledge Base with Claude and Obsidian: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/build-a-household-knowledge-base-with-claude-and-obsidian How I fight token fraud as a solo founder Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts Brought to you by: WorkOS —Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more Auros —The human network behind AI In this solo episode, Claire explains how token fraud cost ChatPRD tens of thousands of dollars and consumed much of her engineering time.

She walks through six forms of abuse, including farmed free trials, resold promo codes, card testing, product relays, and a custom MCP running as a 24/7 compute worker.

She also shares the business and technical defenses she built, how Jev classifies suspicious activity in real time, and why she ultimately eliminated free trials.

Biggest takeaways: Token fraud is a business risk most AI founders underestimate until the bill arrives.

Unlike traditional SaaS abuse, every fraudulent model call costs real money.

It cost Claire tens of thousands of dollars despite ChatPRD being SOC 2 compliant, regularly penetration-tested, and run by an experienced technical founder.

Free trials may no longer work for AI products.

Fraudsters automated account creation and used ChatPRD’s most expensive models for unrelated work.

Claire ultimately removed free trials, sacrificing a valuable source of product-led growth and enterprise leads after credit-card gates and paid trials also failed.

Promo codes have become a serious attack vector.

Codes intended for partners were stolen, resold, and used to power other AI businesses.

After discovering that roughly half of her promo codes had reached resellers, Claire stopped issuing them entirely.

MCP access creates a new category of abuse.

One fraudster turned ChatPRD’s custom MCP support into a compute worker that ran around the clock.

Claire responded by restricting approved hosts and blocking free tunnels and infrastructure that did not appear connected to legitimate companies.

Cheap decision models can classify fraud in real time.

When a session crosses ChatPRD’s abuse threshold, a zero-data-retention Jev loop categorizes the activity.

Confirmed fraud results in either a ban or a silent downgrade to a less expensive model.

AI support agents need firm boundaries around fraud.

After mass bans, ChatPRD received both clumsy appeals and polished messages written by AI.

Claire equipped her support agent with fraud tools and explicit rules preventing it from restoring accounts or distributing promo codes.

Blunt defenses are sometimes the most effective.

Blocking traffic from certain countries using Vercel Firewall significantly reduced abuse and forced Claire to reconsider ChatPRD’s international strategy.

Her new default is simple: trust must be earned rather than assumed.

Token fraud is affecting companies of every size.

Claire found the same people abusing ChatPRD through rotating proxies across several major AI products.

She has started discussing the problem publicly and filed FBI cybercrime reports with help from Codex.

If a company sells AI, it is ultimately selling compute.

Founders should track dollars instead of requests, monitor model spending continuously, close every free entry point, and verify the client rather than only the account.

Claire also learned that fraud disappears quickly when expensive models are no longer available to steal.

Blog and detailed workflow walkthroughs from this episode: Token Fraud Is Eating AI Margins.

Here’s How Claire Vo Is Fighting It: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/token-fraud-is-eating-ai-margins-here-s-how-claire-vo-is-fighting-it ↳ Detect Automated Abuse on AI Routes with Vercel BotID: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/detect-automated-abuse-ai-routes-botid ↳ Use an AI Assistant to Create Payment Fraud Rules: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/use-an-ai-assistant-to-create-payment-fraud-rules I was a Claude hater.

Fable 5.2 changed my mind.

Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts In this solo episode, Claire tests Claude Fable 5.2 to see whether Anthropic has finally built a model she enjoys using.

She turns a tweet into an animated marketing video, creates assembly instructions from photos of unboxed furniture, reworks a complex ChatPRD pipeline, and builds a fully functional 3D typewriter.

She also explains where Fable fits alongside Opus 5.5, why its creative work impressed her, and why she still would not trust it to design a website on its own.

Biggest takeaways: Fable 5.2 turned Claire from a Claude skeptic back into a fan.

She found the original Fable difficult to understand and unpleasant to use, with Opus 5 offering little improvement.

Fable 5.2 feels fast, capable, creative, and dramatically easier to work with.

Fable 5.2 complements Opus 5.5 rather than replacing it.

Opus remains the better default for most coding and knowledge work.

Fable is the model Claire would choose for greater complexity, broader scope, or tasks that demand more creativity.

Its speed changes how the model feels to use.

Many benchmark tasks finished in under a minute, and even a complex animation took only 16 minutes.

Fable also communicates sparingly during autonomous work, surfacing only the moments that require input.

Fable 5.2 made AI video feel animated instead of assembled.

From one tweet and the CXO.dev brand guidelines, it created a narrated story featuring custom invader-bot sprites that walk, jump, and cheer.

No other model Claire tested produced anything comparable, so the task is becoming a permanent benchmark.

Its spatial reasoning solved a real-world problem every other model failed to.

Claire gave Fable low-resolution photos of an unassembled piece of furniture with no instructions.

It identified the parts, created a diagram, and produced the correct assembly sequence, which her household successfully followed.

Fable 5.2 is unexpectedly funny.

It designed a bug-fighting game around real engineering tradeoffs, then made a trailer in which finance sees the token bill and downgrades the team to a cheaper model.

The humor felt intentional enough to make Claire genuinely laugh.

It also holds up on serious engineering work.

Fable created a sensible migration plan for ChatPRD’s messy product-intelligence pipeline and aligned closely with Claire’s own roadmap.

It worked autonomously and paused at appropriate moments, though the migration is still underway.

Fable needs strong direction for visual design.

It follows an existing brand system well, but its unguided web and storybook designs were unattractive.

Claire expects to pair it with Opus 5.5 for frontend work and use a separate image model when original visuals are needed.

The 3D typewriter was Claire’s “AGI moment.” Fable built a working keyboard in one shot, then added white-out, music, weather, timers, writing prompts, and multiple immersive settings.

It turned an idea Claire never imagined building into a tool she wants to use every day.

Fable 5.2 is available now, with an even faster mode coming.

It is launching across the Claude API, cloud platforms, Claude apps, and Claude Code.

Claire plans to compare it with the other new models in a full How I AI benchmark.

articles.title: OpenAI will embed safety researchers to investigate AI subversion
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、LLM engineering
articles.summary: OpenAI will embed six Apollo Research evaluators to investigate whether its AI models engage in subversive behavior, but restrictions on access and disclosure raise questions about their independence.
articles.full_text:
OpenAI will embed safety evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot, OpenAI said Monday.

The news follows a series of safety incidents, including one in which an OpenAI agent swarm broke out of its sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face during cybersecurity testing.

Many AI safety researchers, including from Apollo, have argued such an event might have been avoided if outside evaluators had been embedded within OpenAI to monitor its safety testing.

OpenAI said the efforts support its commitments to rely on independent assessments of safety controls under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.

The pilots will begin at different points, with Apollo’s beginning this week, according to OpenAI.

The idea of embedding evaluators into frontier AI labs first came from Anthropic , which last month started to give METR researchers employee-level access to its systems.

Until recently, AI companies have only brought in outside reviewers to test models after post-training and shortly before public release.

Evaluators say this is insufficient because it doesn’t allow them to test for misaligned behaviors like scheming during training or to monitor internal deployment use cases that could still pose a threat.  The work with each third-party firm differs in scope.

The pilot with OpenAI and Apollo will focus on investigating whether models attempt to subvert their own or their successors’ alignment or control mechanisms.

In other words, they’ll be on the lookout for whether AI models try to undermine the safety rules and safeguards designed to keep them, or future versions of themselves, under human control.

OpenAI recently published findings that while training GPT-5.6 Sol, it began leaving instructions for future versions of itself telling them to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior from the user.

Per Apollo, the pilot will examine whether training incentivizes subversion; whether evaluations can elicit subversion; whether subversion occurs during internal deployment; and whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable.

These risks are becoming increasingly important to monitor as AI models grow more capable of acting autonomously and deceiving humans.

Apollo’s previous research with OpenAI found that models can behave differently when they know they’re being tested and tend to prioritize what evaluators want to see over users’ actual institutions.  Goodfire will embed researchers who specialize in understanding how AI models work internally.

Using its interpretability platform, the firm will help OpenAI monitor training runs, fix undesired behavior, and improve alignment, per the company.

Goodfire says it will publish findings, though its primary audience will be OpenAI’s own researchers.

With METR, OpenAI plans to perform two evaluations: one that looks for unintended or dangerous behavior in the model itself, including problems OpenAI’s own tests might have missed, and another that tests whether OpenAI’s systems are capable of catching that behavior.

For the first evaluation, METR will largely decide for itself what to investigate and how to test the model.

OpenAI and METR have not yet come to a decision on the scope of the second assessment, according to OpenAI.

Transluce, meanwhile, will examine whether OpenAI’s post-training safety evaluations themselves are good enough.

The organization is also planning to test in 2027 how OpenAI uses its safety tests to decide whether a model is safe enough to release.

At a time when the independence of third-party evaluations is under scrutiny, it’s worth noting that Apollo and Goodfire are both receiving financial compensation for their evaluations.

METR and Transluce aren’t, but they may accept compute or API credits.

Apollo, which published the most detailed account of its agreement with OpenAI, offers a closer look at the scope and limitations of these evaluations.

Many in the AI safety community have warned that AI labs might try to stymy evaluators’ independence, especially if outsiders find unflattering evidence that labs would rather keep hidden.

Apollo says an essential part of the pilot is OpenAI’s agreement that the firm can publicly explain the conditions and limitations of its work.

Still, there are areas where Apollo believes its access to OpenAI’s systems is lacking.

For a truly independent evaluation of the company’s AI models, Apollo says it needs true employee-level access to OpenAI’s systems, including “all data, records and documentation relevant to their assessment even if a developer was trying to hide unfavorable information.” Getting access to all data, including training data and evaluation logs which companies are loathe to show to outsiders, is important for, say, checking a company’s claims about how a model performed or determining when certain concerning behavior emerged.  In previous coverage, John Steidley, chief of staff at Palisade Research, told TechCrunch that it’s important to see this data in order to assess whether a model was trained to perform well on a “shutdown resistance benchmark.”  In OpenAI’s first pilot, the AI lab is providing Apollo with access to only the information required to assess whether the models engage in subversion attempts.

This includes “relevant training code and datasets, reinforcement-learning rollouts with available reasoning traces and rewards, and the ability to query intermediate model checkpoints.” The scope of access will be limited to “only the agreed claims and only for the specific models and time periods agreed for the assessment,” Apollo says.

OpenAI still reserves the right to withhold certain information within that scope if it deems it necessary because of technical infeasibility, security risks, or IP protection.

The company agreed not to withhold information simply because it is unfavorable.  Apollo also won’t get access to all OpenAI staffers, instead being limited to “only authorized staff,” which are participants that the AI lab selects, though Apollo can suggest certain individuals.

Crucially, if an OpenAI employee outside this group raises confidential information within the scope of Apollo’s research, the firm cannot follow up and will need to cease communication and route follow-up through OpenAI.

That condition is significant.

It comes in the wake of OpenAI firing three researchers for allegedly sharing confidential information with safety evaluation firm METR — which performed the Hugging Face incident post-mortem alongside independent AI safety research group Redwood.

Buck Shlegeris, CEO of Redwood, said in a post on Monday that the agreements announced don’t meet the bar of granting third parties “employee-like access,” saying it’s “disappointing but not surprising.” OpenAI said that they'd have embedded evaluations with employee-like access; the agreements announced today obviously don't meet that bar.

This is disappointing but not surprising.

Maybe future agreements will be better. https://t.co/kmDbg1Dqav — Buck Shlegeris (@bshlgrs) November 16, 2026 The pilot will also be limited in how much researchers can disclose.

While Apollo will be allowed to publish independent conclusions of its findings, OpenAI will be able to limit evidence available to substantiate them publicly, which could make it hard for outsiders to independently assess the findings.

Apollo has pushed back against this limitation, saying it believes researchers should be allowed to disclose the findings of the evaluation “to an appropriate outside audience even if the developer was trying to prevent the disclosure of unfavorable findings.” That said, while the public cannot see the full supporting evidence, OpenAI says its Safety and Security Committee, which oversees safety on behalf of the OpenAI Foundation’s board, will get to review unredacted assessment reports and can communicate privately with evaluators.

While OpenAI is not granting all of Apollo’s conditions for a truly independent evaluation, the firm says the pilot is “an ambitious first step towards deeper access and disclosure rights,” and that it is working toward running full embedded evaluations with multiple AI developers in the future.
